rules.text: Shared rules apply to every project; service rules additionally apply to service projects, and project-specific authoritative documents may only add or tighten constraints. Preload and recheck baseline rules, but apply conditional rules only when their type or technology is relevant; never introduce unnecessary types, modules, or dependencies solely to satisfy an inapplicable rule.
Before changing a service, read the project documentation entry declared by its project guidance, then read every authoritative document routed for the task.
Before changing domain boundaries, language, business rules, errors, domain events, or API business semantics, read the service's authoritative domain document.
Use Java 17.
Module dependency cycles are forbidden; fix responsibilities or extract a shared module rather than hiding a cycle through reflection or events.
Inner modules must not depend on outer protocols, persistence implementations, persistence objects, or the boot module.
Keep domain rules in domain, use-case orchestration in application, technical adapters in infrastructure, protocol handling in interfaces, and runtime assembly in boot.
Never modify, reuse, or reassign a published error code.
Run verification proportional to the change and do not claim completion without reporting the commands and results.

skills.name: develop-service
skills.when: Developing, changing, or reviewing service code under the shared engineering standards during development

rules.text: Each module declares only the minimum dependencies required by its current compile-time and runtime semantics.
Module cycles are forbidden; remove them by extracting a shared module or correcting responsibility boundaries, never by hiding the cycle with reflection or events.

The service parent POM must declare every service module except test-only modules and the boot assembly module under `<dependencyManagement><dependencies>`, using `${project.version}`. Do not declare those modules as direct parent-POM dependencies, because direct dependencies are inherited by child modules and would violate module dependency boundaries.
Only concrete technical implementations, runtime adapters, and final assembly modules may depend on aggregate starters; other modules use the smallest capability artifact.
Before adding dependencies, assess maintenance, security, license, and dependency cost.
Do not add functionally overlapping dependencies when existing dependencies meet the need.
Choose scope by actual use: compile for compilation requirements, test for tests, and provided only for capabilities genuinely supplied by the runtime.
Use optional only for a genuinely optional capability; it is not a replacement for choosing the correct scope.
SNAPSHOT dependencies are forbidden in release branches and production builds and may only be temporary in local or unpublished iteration branches.
Manage third-party versions centrally; business and feature modules must not override versions independently.
Use the unified service version pair: Spring Boot `3.5.16` with Spring Cloud `2025.0.3`.
Upgrade the version pair with `framework-dependencies` and update the policy table in the same release.
Use `framework-dependencies` and `framework-starter-dependencies` for centralized versions, selecting `framework-*` contracts and `framework-starter-*` implementations as needed.
Technology-neutral domain and application modules depend only on the minimum framework contracts required by their responsibility.
Select replaceable persistence, messaging, and scheduling implementations through boot packaging dependencies.
Do not switch multiple technology implementations inside one artifact using runtime properties.
Compile and run with Java 17.
Production code must not use `var`, including local variables, loop variables, try-with-resources variables, and lambda parameters; use an explicit type wherever a type declaration is needed.

Only test source sets may use `var`, and only when the initializer itself clearly shows the concrete type; declare the type explicitly when determining it requires reading a called method declaration or relying on generic type inference. Test source sets include unit tests, integration tests, and dedicated test support; a type in production sources is not exempt merely because its name contains `Test`.
Prefer `record` for data carriers whose state is complete at construction, remains immutable, and does not require inheritance, proxies, or JavaBean setter binding.
Defensively copy collection record components with `List.copyOf`, `Set.copyOf`, or the corresponding immutable-copy operation.
Use an ordinary class when the type requires inheritance, mutable state, framework proxying, JavaBean shape, or complex domain behavior.
Prefer wrapper types such as `Integer`, `Long`, and `Boolean`; use primitives only for intentional default values, performance characteristics, or explicitly non-null semantics.

In both production and test code, always use braces for the bodies of `if`, `else`, `for` (including enhanced for), `while`, and `do-while`, even for a single statement or an empty body; never use a lone semicolon as an empty body. An `else if` chain is allowed, but every conditional branch body must still use braces.
For simple collection traversal, `forEach` is an available concise style; choose it only when it remains immediately readable.
For simple transformations and callbacks, Stream, lambdas, and method references are available concise styles; choose them only when they remain immediately readable.
Prefer `Optional` for possibly absent return values and chained handling.
Do not use `Optional` as a Bean property or method parameter.
For complex business rules, nested conditions, and exception flows, prioritize readability over functional style.

Do not hard-code string literals carrying business meaning, requiring existing cross-class reuse, or identifying business branches or states; configuration defaults are exempt. Stable protocol keys follow their adapter rules. Purely local technical separators with no business/protocol convention or cross-class reuse may remain literals; hypothetical future reuse alone does not require extraction.
Represent a fixed, closed value set such as finite states or categories with an enum.
Represent a single value shared across classes with a `public static final` constant or a dedicated constants type.
Externalize deployment-varying values as configuration; defaults are allowed.

A log message, non-business diagnostic exception message, test fixture value, regular expression, or format template may remain a literal only when it carries no business meaning, does not drive branching or state, and needs no cross-class reuse.
Prefer the JDK, an already-used framework, or a mature maintained library over reimplementing general technical capabilities.
Distinguish null-only, non-empty, and non-blank before selecting a predicate; never change semantics to standardize tools. Treat null and empty collections alike only when the scenario allows it.

In modules already depending on Spring, use semantics-matching utilities: `StringUtils.hasLength` for non-empty strings, `hasText` for non-blank strings, and `CollectionUtils.isEmpty` when null and empty collections are equivalent. Use null comparisons or JDK equivalents for null-only checks.
A module decoupled from Spring must not add Spring Framework only for utility methods.

When the JDK is insufficient in a Spring-decoupled module, use managed Commons tools matching the predicate semantics: strings use `isEmpty`/`isNotEmpty` or `isBlank`/`isNotBlank`; collections use collections4 `isEmpty`/`isNotEmpty` only when null and empty are equivalent.
Do not hand-write logic equivalent to the utilities above.
When dependencies and runtime validation are available, prefer Jakarta Bean Validation for nullability, format, and range constraints on bindable properties and method parameters or returns.
When using Bean Validation, declare constraints at the corresponding field, property, record component, parameter, or return location and ensure the actual call path triggers validation.
`@Valid` marks cascaded validation of nested objects and is not itself a constraint.

Use explicit checks when Bean Validation cannot express the constraint, the call path cannot guarantee validation, or an explicit business-error meaning is required; this includes constructors and factories outside framework binding that need fast failure.

Technical preconditions detect programming errors or protect internal technical invariants. They must not use service business error codes; general technical exceptions or `FrameworkException` with framework-wide technical codes are allowed.

Choose explicit-check tools by failure semantics first, then available dependencies and capability, in order: framework-core `Require`, Spring `Assert`, managed Commons `Validate`, and JDK checks such as `Objects.requireNonNull`. Advance only when the preceding tool is unavailable or unsuitable; handwrite checks only when existing tools and the JDK cannot satisfy the requirement.

Do not add dependencies solely for explicit checks or hand-write equivalent logic already provided by an available tool that satisfies the failure semantics; dependency selection follows the common-utilities rules.
Classify exceptions by failure semantics rather than merely inheritance from `BaseException`.
Service business errors use bound Chinese templates; project-authored technical diagnostics and Bean Validation messages use English. Original third-party messages are exempt.
Determine business outcomes by stable business error codes; never parse an exception message as a stable protocol.
Handle or propagate business exceptions and never silently ignore an exception; non-business exception logging follows the logging rules.

references.title: Layered Service Validation and Exception Rules

rules.text: Use `@Valid` for request-object entries with the default validation group and `@Validated` for explicitly selected groups; never stack both indiscriminately at the same entry.
Prefer declaring public API method-parameter and return-value constraints on the API interface or API data type.
Implementations must not duplicate or strengthen parameter constraints declared by a public API interface.
Trigger Spring MVC request-object validation through entry-parameter `@Valid`, or `@Validated` for specific groups; follow the entry group-selection rules.
Direct MVC parameter constraints such as `@NotBlank` or `@Min` use MVC method validation; do not blanket-annotate Controllers with class-level `@Validated` merely to enable it.

For method-parameter or return-value validation on a regular Spring Bean such as a Facade or application service, put `@Validated` on the concrete Bean implementation and invoke it through the Spring proxy; the interface declares contract constraints and the implementation enables runtime method validation.

Business checks express expected business rejections and must throw an exception extending framework-core `BaseException` with a stable business code, through a Require exception supplier or an explicit throw. Tool fallback must preserve that meaning; ordinary technical preconditions must not use business exception suppliers.

A `Require.valid` predicate uses its passed `value` as the sole input: it may call value methods, reference `static final` constants or class literals, and use immutable values derived solely from `value` inside the predicate. Never capture other variables, parameters, instance fields, or mutable external state.
Use explicit guards for cross-variable checks, never `Require.valid`; classify their exceptions by failure semantics rather than treating every cross-variable decision as a technical precondition.
Use `Require.notNull`/`allNotNull` only for constructor parameters and public-method parameters, not return values, local variables, or fields.
For Require parameter null checks, use `notNull` for one parameter and `allNotNull` for multiple parameters; do not chain repeated `notNull` calls.
Technical null-element checks cover collection elements and both Map keys and values; any null element throws `FrameworkException`. This rule does not replace domain or business validity checks.
Prefer `NullSafe.forEach` for null-element checking alone; prefer `NullSafe.copyOf` when an immutable copy is also needed, without a redundant `forEach` check.

Prefer Jakarta Bean Validation for API field-shape constraints; a check returns a business error only when the API contract explicitly promises that error semantics. Execute the check at its responsibility boundary rather than moving it into API or protocol code because the API exposes the error.
Validate rules that depend on domain state, persistence data, or use-case context in application or domain rather than moving them to the protocol-binding layer.
Translate Jakarta Bean Validation failures into the framework exception hierarchy at the unified exception translation boundary.
Service-defined business exceptions extend framework-core `BaseException`, never JDK `RuntimeException` or other JDK exceptions directly.

Guards expressing domain rules or domain validity throw `DomainException` extending `BaseException`, not generic JDK exceptions. Programming errors and technical preconditions inside domain remain technical exceptions; location alone does not make them business failures.
Each domain's `DomainException` provides `invalidEntityId()` for invalid domain entity identifiers. The error-code policy exclusively defines the code allocation for `DOMAIN_ENTITY_ID_INVALID`.
Do not use annotations from `lombok.experimental`.
Do not use `@Builder`; use explicit constructors or factory methods for staged or fluent construction.

Generate constructors that only assign fields and contain no validation, transformation, or initialization logic with Lombok constructor annotations rather than writing them manually; write an explicit constructor when such logic exists.

Generate getters and setters that only read or assign fields and contain no validation, transformation, or other behavior with Lombok `@Getter` or `@Setter`; write methods explicitly when behavior exists.
Use `@Slf4j` instead of declaring a Logger field manually.
Aggregate roots and entities use only `@Getter` for field access; prohibit `@Data` and externally exposed setters without domain behavior.
Implement aggregate-root and entity equality explicitly from unique identity; do not use Lombok `@EqualsAndHashCode`.
When a value object is an ordinary class, use final fields, getters, an appropriate all-arguments constructor, and full-field equality.
Spring Beans use final dependencies and constructor injection, normally through `@RequiredArgsConstructor`.
Declare loggers under the Lombok rules and use SLF4J placeholders instead of concatenating message text.
When logging an exception, pass the exception object as the last argument instead of embedding it in message text.

Choose severity by impact and handling: ERROR for failures requiring human intervention such as exhausted retries, unrecoverable or unclassified integrity failures; WARN for noteworthy abnormal contention, recovery, or degradation; INFO for normal idempotency and key business/external-interaction audit points; DEBUG for diagnosis. Exception translation alone does not make a normal idempotent hit WARN.
Disable DEBUG in production by default.
Include locatable business context such as use-case/job name, sanitized business key, and scene or shard identifier.
Let the framework inject tracing context; business code must not manually assemble trace fields.
Logs must not replace metrics, alerts, or distributed tracing.

Aggregate, rate-limit, or sample high-frequency recurring operational records instead of INFO per occurrence or escalation to WARN to bypass controls. Aggregates retain scene, time window, count, and outcome.
Explicit per-event audit records must use a controlled audit channel without sampling or loss.

Sensitive data means passwords, tokens, keys, certificates, government IDs, phone numbers, bank-card numbers, biometrics, precise addresses, and similar personal data, plus complete request or response payloads.
Never emit sensitive data in plain text in message text, parameters, MDC, or exception information.
Correlate sensitive business keys only through centralized masking or irreversible digests; do not scatter such implementations in business code.

When a log must reference a sensitive business key, use the centrally implemented masking or irreversible digest; do not scatter masking logic across business code, keep the data type recognizable while masking the value itself (for example a phone number as `138****1234`), and keep one consistent mask format per sensitive type.
Use MapStruct for structural mappings between data carriers with corresponding fields; do not hand-write field copying or use `BeanUtils.copyProperties`.

Use explicit semantic methods for domain construction, business validation, state transitions, and protocol encoding; a MapStruct mapper may call those methods but must not hide them in automatic field mapping.

Define a conversion contract independently; a handwritten `@Mapper` interface extends it or abstract class implements it, using `@Override` when redeclaring contract methods. The handwritten mapper follows the naming rules.
MapStruct generates concrete implementations at compile time; never handwrite or modify generated classes.
Reuse existing mappers through `@Mapper(uses = {...})` instead of duplicating field-level conversions.
Declare `componentModel = spring` and `unmappedTargetPolicy = ERROR` in shared `@MapperConfig`, reference it via each mapper's `config`, and retain these shared defaults.
For ordinary mappings, explicitly declare `ignore = true` for each intentionally unmapped target field.

For partial-update or projection whitelists, use method-level `@BeanMapping(ignoreByDefault = true)` and explicit allowed mappings; never substitute local `unmappedTargetPolicy = IGNORE` or disable missing-mapping checks.
Keep generic converters and helpers private to mapper use and do not expose them as business components.

Read authoritative project documents before changing layering, domain boundaries, or API business semantics; project rules may add or tighten shared rules but must not duplicate, relax, or override them.
`<service>-api` defines stable external API contracts.
`<service>-domain` owns the core domain model and rules.
`<service>-application` orchestrates write use cases and read-only queries.

`<service>-infrastructure` contains technical adapters, persistence abstractions, and technology-neutral shared conversions, but no DOs or conversion mappers tied to a concrete persistence technology.

Concrete persistence, scheduler, and message implementations live in `<service>-infrastructure-persistence-<technology>`, `<service>-infrastructure-scheduler-<technology>`, and `<service>-infrastructure-message-<technology>` modules.

A persistence implementation module owns that stack's DOs, DO conversion mappers, repositories, and SQL/XML loading, assembly, and verification; physical resource placement follows the project configuration directory rules.
`<service>-interfaces` implements protocol-neutral Facades and hosts REST, RPC, and message subscription adapters.
`<service>-openfeign-client` provides the OpenFeign client for the service API.
`<service>-boot` starts, configures, and packages the service.

The standalone `<service>-integration-tests` module verifies collaboration among real implementations from multiple modules, full auto-configuration, and real databases or middleware. Merely referencing another module's interfaces or DTOs does not make a test an integration test; production modules must not depend on this module.

Top-level packages must match the module responsibility, such as `api`, `domain`, `application`, `infrastructure`, or `interfaces`; do not place production types from different layers or technology adapters directly in the module root package.

Package dependencies must follow the service layer dependency direction; package boundaries must not bypass module constraints or hide reverse dependencies through cross-package access, reflection, or events.
Within a layer, group packages by business capability or technical adapter before role subpackages; do not create global `entity`, `service`, or `repository` buckets by default.

The `infrastructure` module must further group packages by capability or adapter boundary, such as `persistence`, `messaging`, `locking`, `external`, or `configuration`; do not place all adapters, DOs, mappers, configuration, and clients in one `infra` package.

A concrete technology module groups packages first by technology stack and then by aggregate, resource, or external service; technology-specific DOs, repositories, conversion mappers, and assembly may share a feature package or its role subpackages, but concrete DOs and technology annotations must not be shared across stacks.
Cross-capability reuse must use a stable port, contract, or explicit shared component; do not couple capabilities through another feature package's implementation classes, database DOs, or mappers.

Create a subpackage only when its types form a clear responsibility boundary; do not create a package for a single type merely for visual symmetry, and split oversized packages by capability or reason for change rather than mechanically by class name.

Keep implementation types package-private by default; declare a type `public` only when cross-package, cross-module, or framework assembly requires it, and give every public type an explicit contract or adapter responsibility.
Mirror production package paths in tests by default.
Keep test helpers in test sources or test-support packages; never place them in production packages or make production code depend on them.
API must not depend on business implementations.
Domain must not depend on other business layers.
Application depends on domain; any additional contract dependencies follow the application boundary rules.
Infrastructure implements domain and application ports; concrete persistence, scheduler, and message modules depend on infrastructure.
Interfaces depends on API and application.
OpenFeign client depends on API.
Boot depends on modules required for runtime assembly and performs final assembly only.
Integration-tests may depend on boot and observed service modules in test scope only; those verification dependencies never participate in production dependency direction.
No inner module may depend on outer protocol types, persistence objects, concrete technologies, or boot.

Determine ownership from authoritative project responsibility/domain documents and business semantics, not names, packages, annotations, or branch counts. Protocol parsing, serialization, connection management, and technical retries that preserve business semantics are adapter behavior. Classify gateway protocol authentication and route execution by their actual semantics rather than automatically moving them into domain/application.

Locate where eligibility decisions, business invariants, state transitions, and business decisions actually execute. Keep each rule in its owning domain model or domain service and reuse it across entry points; controllers, filters, listeners, adapters, and application must not maintain independent copies of domain decisions. Distinguish protocol-format validation from domain validity using the validation rules.

Trace use-case call chains to locate business step ordering, coordination of domain capabilities or ports, business-result branching, and business compensation decisions; application owns this orchestration. Multiple SDK calls, page fetching, or technical retries within one adapter operation do not alone imply application orchestration; independent infrastructure recovery follows the compensation rules.

Do not treat the existence of domain/application modules or an intermediate forwarding service as proof of cohesion; trace the implementation that actually decides and orchestrates. Responsibility migration must move the decisions and their behavioral verification, not merely move classes, rename packages, or add forwarding layers while leaving business logic in outer layers.

Check dependency direction in declared/inherited POM dependencies and source imports, fully qualified type references, method signatures, inheritance/implementation relationships, and injected types; trace related call chains for implicit reverse dependencies. Apply the allowed layer dependencies and type boundaries, not merely successful compilation, absence of cycles, or use of interfaces.
Create a root-level `config/` directory beside service modules as the preferred home for independently updateable resources.
Prefer the project-root `config/` directory for project-level application configuration, MyBatis SQL/XML, database schema or migrations, Dubbo XML, and other independently updateable resources.
Do not package an independently updateable configuration resource in a module artifact merely because that module assembles the capability.

Associate external SQL, mappings, schema, and other configuration resources with application versions and verify compatibility before deployment; independent deployment never removes code-version compatibility requirements.

Explicitly load root-level `config/` resources through `spring.config.location`, `spring.config.additional-location`, `spring.config.import`, technology-specific location settings, or equivalent startup parameters.
Build, deployment, and local startup must provide required external resources and verify expected failure for missing or invalid configuration.

Package resources in module `src/main/resources` only when external loading is unsupported, resource/code versions or classpaths are inseparable, or deployment cannot provide an artifact's mandatory self-contained resources. Development convenience alone is not sufficient.

When a `*Properties` type already provides a default value and the configuration file does not change it, the configuration file must not restate the property; configuration files carry only explicit decisions that differ from code defaults and externally varying values.

Configuration properties must not introduce environment-variable placeholders by default and must not require the deployment environment to provide a variable by default; when injection is genuinely needed, the deployment configuration or a dedicated profile carries it, and a missing value must fail fast.
API defines stable Facade-centered contracts and contains interfaces and contract types without business implementations.
API may contain command, query, response, event, enum, and constants packages; enums represent finite values and constants represent headers, topics, event types, and similar fixed values.
Facade inputs implement `Request` and use complete immutable API command/query records independent of HTTP binding and header injection.
Facade outputs use `Result<T>` or paged `PageResult<T>`; use `Result<Void>` for no payload and `Result<List<T>>` for nonpaged collections.
API integration events implement `IntegrationEvent`; they may be mapped from domain events but must use distinct types.
Use aggregate roots as consistency boundaries and define entities, value objects, domain services, repository contracts, and domain events around the domain model.

A domain entity identifier extends `EntityId`. Each project provides type-specific bases such as `StringEntityId` and `LongEntityId`, centralizes value-type validation by overriding `validate()`, and overrides it again in a concrete identifier only for additional constraints.
Aggregate roots and entities change state only through domain behavior.
Value objects are immutable.
Domain services contain only cross-aggregate rules or rules not belonging to a single aggregate.

Domain-service `*Effect` result types implement `DomainEffect` and return the domain events produced by that behavior through `events()`; return an empty collection rather than null when no event is produced.

Domain objects and services must not call system time directly; application services inject `Clock`, obtain business time once per use case, and pass the same value to related state changes and events.
Domain repositories express domain-object persistence contracts without exposing a persistence technology.
Domain behavior decides occurrence and business content; raw domain events contain occurrence time, event type, and business content only, without EventStore record IDs or ID-generator dependencies.
EventStore generates a global ID when building `DomainEventEnvelope`, used only for persistence, publication, tracing, and idempotency.

Define an outbound port in domain when the external capability is part of the domain model and directly serves a domain rule; design its contract with domain-semantic types rather than the external service protocol.

Domain must not know API payloads, application commands/outputs/views, external-service payloads, HTTP or third-party SDK types, persistence DOs, concrete technologies, `Result<T>`, or `PageResult<T>`.
Application orchestrates use cases, coordinates domain objects and ports, and does not implement domain rules.
Command services are write-use-case entry points, accept application commands, return command outputs or void, and own transaction boundaries.
Query services are read-only, accept domain IDs, value objects, or query conditions, return application views, and use `PagedList<T>` for pagination.

Define an outbound port in application when the external capability serves only use-case orchestration, flow coordination, or a query and is not part of the domain model or domain rules; use local application or domain semantic types in its contract.

Application may depend on domain, API integration-event contracts, and framework ports, but not API command/query/response types, protocol implementations, persistence DOs, external-service payloads, HTTP types, or third-party SDK types.

references.title: Infrastructure, Interfaces, Client, and Boot Rules

rules.text: Infrastructure provides repository, ID, event-storage, messaging, scheduling, and other technical adapters and implements ports defined by domain or application without owning domain rules or use-case orchestration.

Adapt domain-event storage through the framework-domain port; domain and application must not depend on a concrete event-store implementation. Envelope identity follows the domain-event and distributed-ID rules.
For JavaBean configuration binding, collection and nested-object fields are final, expose getters without setters, and begin as empty binding containers without business defaults.
Required configuration collections use `@NotEmpty` so missing configuration fails startup rather than running silently with an empty value.
For an independent Duration minimum, use both `@NotNull` and `@DurationMin` with explicit units.
A module using `@DurationMin` directly declares `hibernate-validator`.
Use `@AssertTrue` and similar type-level validation only for relationships between fields.
Reuse infrastructure Beans supplied by the runtime framework instead of declaring another Bean with the same semantics.
Interfaces provides protocol-neutral Facade implementations and REST, RPC, and message entry points without domain rules or use-case orchestration.
Facade implementations convert API/application objects, call application services, and wrap responses with `Result<T>` or `PageResult<T>`.
Controllers handle routing, binding, and necessary protocol context only, convert the HTTP request into an API command/query, then invoke a Facade contract.
Inject or resolve Client, Channel, Device, and other HTTP header context only in interfaces; API, application, and domain must not depend on the HTTP header binding mechanism.
After header injection and validation, each controller business request converges into one ordinary mutable `@Valid` HTTP request extending `ClientRequest`.
Implement the composable `ChannelContext` and `AuthenticatedSessionContext` only when the endpoint really needs trusted channel or authenticated-session context.

Do not split business fields into path or query parameters alongside a separate client-context argument; for endpoints without a business body, declare a concrete request type matching the required contexts and let the shared argument resolver build and validate it from protected headers.
After header injection and validation, interfaces converts its mutable HTTP request into a complete immutable API command/query record; Facades must not accept interfaces HTTP request types.
Publish the same Facade Bean directly when the RPC technology supports it; add a technology-specific RPC adapter only for incompatible models, semantics, metadata, or exception handling.
Message listeners are interfaces-layer protocol entries and are not required to pass through a Facade; messaging rules own consumption reliability and processing flow.
OpenFeign clients match Facade method signatures, reuse API contract types and response wrappers, and contain no business model, use case, or conversion rules.
Boot owns startup, runtime configuration, and packaging; dependency rules own technology implementation selection.
Boot contains no domain rules, application orchestration, protocol adapters, or business types.
Use records for API response payloads.
Use a record for an API event when serialization, RPC, OpenFeign, and clients support constructor binding; use an ordinary JavaBean class when an existing consumer cannot support it.
For public Java APIs, evaluate the binary-constructor compatibility impact before adding a record component.
Prefer records for domain IDs, value objects, effects, and immutable events when inheritance is unnecessary.
Use ordinary classes for aggregate roots, entities, mutable state, or complex behavior, following the Java type-selection rules.

Use ordinary mutable classes for interfaces HTTP requests so JSON binding and Client, Channel, or Device header injection can populate them; they may extend the required Client context type but must not be used as Facade inputs.
Prefer records for immutable application commands, outputs, query conditions, and views.
Services, repositories, gateways, and mappers use ordinary classes or their corresponding interfaces, never records.
Read-only persistence projections may use records by default.
DOs, JPA entities, and types requiring no-argument constructors or setter mapping use ordinary classes.
Name interfaces by business role, port, or technical contract without `I*` or `*Interface`.
Name abstract classes `Abstract*`; reserve `Base*` for framework or shared base types.
Do not use generic `*Impl`; name implementations by default role, technology, adapter responsibility, or strategy.

Spring Boot auto-configuration entry classes must use the `*AutoConfiguration` suffix. All other types must be named by their actual responsibility without the `Configuration` suffix, except component-scanned wiring classes.
Name component-scanned wiring classes with the `*Configuration` suffix.
Name configuration-property binding classes with the `*Properties` suffix.
Do not suffix payloads, command outputs, query views, or effects with `*Result`; reserve `Result<T>` and `PageResult<T>` for framework response wrappers.
Use `*ApiResponse` only for a shared API payload return type.

Name a locally owned external-service protocol type with the external service name, action or resource, and `RequestPayload` or `ResponsePayload` suffix, such as `GithubSearchRepositoriesRequestPayload`; do not use names such as `RequestPayload` or `CreateRequestPayload` that omit the external-service identity or call semantics.
Name a locally defined internal-service request type `*InternalRequest` when the callee's published API contract cannot be reused.
Name conversion contracts by layer responsibility and handwritten MapStruct mapper types `*MapStructMapper`.
Place the handwritten MapStruct mapper in its contract package's `mapstruct` subpackage.
Name each concrete business-scenario resource-key handler `*KeyResolver`.
Concrete scenario key resolvers extend `AbstractKeyResolver`; runtime responsibilities follow resource-key rules.

Use lowercase package names that express a stable responsibility or change boundary; do not use `misc`, `temp`, or `other`, and do not place business types in generic `util` or `common` packages. Package hierarchy and grouping follow the service layer rules.
Use `*ApiCommand`, `*ApiOutput`, `*ApiQuery`, `*ApiView`, `*ApiEnum`, `*ApiConstants`, `*ApiEvent`, `*CommandFacade`, and `*QueryFacade` in API.
Use `*Effect` for domain-service results, `*Repository` for repository contracts, and `*Event` for domain events.
Use `*CommandService`, `*Command`, `*Output`, `*QueryService`, `*Query`, and `*View` in application; follow the application layering rules for paged return contracts.
Use `*Response` only when an application command and query return type must be reused.
Use `*RepositoryAdapter`, technology-specific `*PersistenceRepository`, `*DO`, and `*PersistenceAutoConfiguration` in infrastructure.
Place protocol-neutral Facade implementations in `interfaces.facade` as `Default*Facade`; use `*RpcAdapter` only for necessary technology-specific RPC adapters.
Name OpenFeign clients `*FeignClient`.
Prefer the callee's published API module and directly reuse request/response contracts rather than redefining equivalents.
Depend only on the callee's public API, never its application, interfaces, or concrete implementation modules.
Define local adapter types only when the published API cannot be referenced or its public contract does not fit the current call boundary.
A local fallback request implements `Request` and follows the internal-request naming rule.
Use `Result<T>` for ordinary fallback responses and `PageResult<T>` for paged responses.

Prefer a fallback response T name consistent with the published contract, but use local semantic names when anti-corruption, protocol, or semantic differences require them; never incorrectly reuse a Java type merely to preserve a name.

Confine external service calls to a local adapter boundary in the concrete infrastructure adapter module and use locally owned request and response types that follow the external-payload naming rule; external SDK types, protocol models, and serialization details must not cross into application or domain, and mapping between local and external models is explicit.

Define typed models for fixed-structure external requests and responses, except the narrowly defined small path/query/header parameter exception; application/json uses `*RequestPayload` and `*ResponsePayload`.
HTTP method and parameter location do not change payload naming; a client adapter, dedicated encoder, or mapper binds payload data to GET query/path/header parameters or POST form/body data.
External-service payloads describe protocol data only and must not implement `queryParams()`, `headers()`, serialization, HTTP parameter assembly, or a dependency on one HTTP client.

A client may directly declare a small fixed set of path/query/header parameters with no reuse need instead of creating a request payload. This exception excludes fixed JSON bodies and responses and never permits assembling fixed fields in a Map.

Use a Map to model an external protocol only when it formally defines dynamic key/value content such as `additionalProperties`, metadata, labels, dynamic identifier keys, runtime-only fields, or uninterpreted extension forwarding.

Use a Map only inside an infrastructure adapter when an SDK or low-level client accepts only a Map, or when form, multipart, or signing input cannot be encoded from a typed payload by the available client.
Use typed payloads for fixed field sets; never use Map merely to save type definitions, reuse a generic request, assemble a few fixed fields, or avoid a mapper.
When Map adaptation is necessary, confine construction and conversion to the matching infrastructure adapter; never expose it through ports or to application/domain.
Use external-service-specific constants for fixed Map protocol keys and keep them in the corresponding infrastructure adapter.
Apply resource-key and namespace rules to business services; framework-internal modules follow their own engineering documentation.
Compose each effective resource name from an application-distinguishing namespace and a business key; deployment infrastructure, not this namespace, provides environment isolation.
A business key is unique only within its namespace; the same business key resolves to a different physical resource in each application.
The namespace expresses application identity only and never carries business meaning; business meaning appears only in the business-key part.

Business code uses business keys only. A scenario `*KeyResolver` owns business prefixes and segments and delegates to injected `ResourceNameResolver`, without parsing or assembling namespaces. Exactly-once namespace injection follows the namespace ownership rules.
Unified infrastructure configuration supplies application namespace identity.
Business code, business configuration, and adapters must not repeat or hand-assemble namespace prefixes for an individual resource; the canonical exactly-once namespace rule owns injection count.

For scenario-assembly namespace injection, make the scenario configuration implement `Namespaced` and inject into its `*KeyResolver` a `NamespacedResourceNameResolver` assembled from that configuration and `NamespaceResolver`.
For final-adapter namespace injection, give the `*KeyResolver` a `ResourceNameResolver` implementation that does not inject a namespace and let the final adapter provide namespace isolation.
Inject a resource namespace exactly once; never combine `NamespacedResourceNameResolver` with a final resource adapter that injects the namespace again.
When a framework entry already resolves a resource name, callers must not resolve or inject its namespace again; distributed-lock key behavior follows the lock rules.
A complete error code has six digits: a three-digit service prefix plus a three-digit local code; error enums declare only the local code, and the framework composes and zero-pads the full code.
One service project represents one bounded context and uses one unique service prefix; independently deployed bounded contexts require distinct prefixes.
A service prefix must be centrally registered and allocated within the deployment system before use; two services in the same deployment system must never use the same prefix.

Choose category, range, prefix, and semantics together: shared DomainError 000-099 / DOMAIN_; aggregate DomainError 100-599 / aggregate name; ApplicationError 600-699 / APP_; own-technology InfrastructureError 700-799 / INFRA_TECH_ (persistence, cache, locks, serialization, files, event storage, outbox); external-adapter InfrastructureError 800-899 / INFRA_ACL_; 900-999 remains unallocated. ACL denotes responsibility, not a required separate module. Aggregate block allocation follows the separate capacity rule.

Aggregate code blocks align to 50-code boundaries (100–149, 150–199, …, 550–599) and 50 codes is the minimum allocation unit. An aggregate exclusively owns every code in all of its assigned blocks and may use one or multiple adjacent blocks. Capacity expansion must reserve additional adjacent, currently unallocated complete blocks; blocks must not be split, shared, or reassigned between aggregates.

Translate an external rejection into `DomainError` or `ApplicationError` when it has a stable local business meaning; do not classify it as infrastructure solely because it originated from another system.
Fix common-domain local code 000 as `DOMAIN_ENTITY_ID_INVALID`; use the category mapping for the shared-domain prefix.
Fix the first two codes of each aggregate's allocated range as `{AGGREGATE}_NOT_FOUND` and `{AGGREGATE}_ALREADY_EXISTS`; the category mapping owns the name prefix.

Error enums live in the module owning their semantics: domain errors in domain, application errors in application, and infrastructure errors in the corresponding infrastructure module. An adapter translating and throwing a domain/application exception does not change that ownership.
Organize and name error enums by owning aggregate, technical mechanism, or the shared-domain segment; do not create one enum mixing code segments from different layers.
A complete error code is globally unique within one deployment system; a local code need only be unique within its service prefix.
Unallocated complete aggregate ranges remain available, but unused codes inside an assigned aggregate range remain owned by that aggregate and must not be reassigned.
Document the service prefix, shared-domain range, and every aggregate range in the authoritative domain document declared by the project documentation entry.
Append new errors in local-code order within the owning range.
Published error codes are immutable and must not be modified, reused, or assigned to a different meaning.

Bind each error code to one stable message template; exception call sites must not replace it, concatenate ad hoc text, or supply an arbitrary message. Dynamic context may fill only parameters declared by the template and must not change the error meaning.
Write stable business-error message templates in Chinese; Jakarta Bean Validation and technical-precondition diagnostics follow the validation-message rule.
Repository adapters translate domain repository contracts to data access, while persistence repositories expose data-access capability only.

The matching persistence implementation module owns concrete JPA, MyBatis, or MyBatis-Plus repositories, DOs, DO conversion mappers, and SQL/XML loading, assembly, and verification. Physical resource placement follows the layered-service configuration rules.

Do not share DO classes across persistence technologies; each JPA, MyBatis, or MyBatis-Plus implementation module owns its DOs with only that technology's required mapping annotations, and DO names follow the naming rules.

Each persistence implementation module owns the conversion mappers between domain objects or application read models and that technology's DOs; do not place converters that depend on concrete DOs in shared infrastructure.

Each persistence implementation module uses one technology; alternative JPA, MyBatis, and MyBatis-Plus implementations may exist in distinct modules but never coexist within one implementation module.
A runtime artifact assembles only one implementation of each repository contract; choose it under the boot packaging-dependency rules.
Replacing MyBatis-Plus with MyBatis must preserve the database schema, table and column names, query semantics, and observable repository behavior.
MyBatis and MyBatis-Plus implementations must load the same shared SQL XML fragments from the project-root `config/` directory.

Declare table names, column lists, and reusable predicates only in shared fragments; concrete mapper statements reference them with `<include>` and must not duplicate them across the two implementations.
For the same logical persistence model, technology-specific JPA, MyBatis, and MyBatis-Plus DOs keep identical business-property names and Java types.

DOs must not declare collection properties or collection-mapping annotations such as `@ElementCollection` and `@CollectionTable`; model multi-value relationships as master/detail DOs and association tables.

Only when the multi-value content is always read and written as a whole and needs no independent query, index, or foreign-key constraint may each technology's DO conversion mapper serialize it into a single string column under consistent conversion rules.

A persistence mapping may declare a logical table name without runtime prefix or suffix; resolve the physical prefix and suffix through the shared naming strategy and never hard-code a deployment-specific physical table name in business code.

Enforce primary keys, business uniqueness, and database-expressible nullability, referential-integrity, and range invariants with schema constraints; application validation and distributed coordination do not replace those constraints, while cross-aggregate, cross-service, and temporal rules remain in domain or application.
Prefer the project-root `config/` directory for `schema.sql` and database migration configuration and load it under the layered-service external-resource rules.
Begin `schema.sql` with a comment requiring table prefix and suffix to match runtime configuration.
A table-prefix or suffix change is a schema change: update DDL or migration configuration along with runtime settings.
Before choosing a concurrency control, assess business risk, actual conflict probability, contention scope, and failure consequences.
For a very-low-contention operational API, omit versions, distributed locks, and pessimistic database locks by default.
When a business state machine or explicit precondition exists, prefer a conditional update on the current state or business condition.
Treat an unexpected conditional-update affected-row count as a state change or concurrency conflict; never overwrite silently.
For a real cross-instance conflict not resolved by business conditions, prefer a distributed lock to reduce contention.
Add version-based optimistic concurrency only when residual conflicts still require detection.
Never apply versions, pessimistic database locks, or distributed locks as a default template for every write.

Keep local-database transactions short and limited to necessary reads and writes; do not perform avoidable RPC, direct message publication, long computation, lock waiting, or multi-batch work inside them.
Every retried write must be idempotent.
Explicitly classify unique-constraint and optimistic-lock conflicts, deadlocks, and transient connection failures; bound retry count rather than retrying indefinitely.
Paginate with a stable unique order and never rely on unspecified database order.
Prefer cursors for deep pagination or continuous scans.
Design indexes by access patterns, data scale, and execution plans; verify plans and acceptable performance before high-frequency or large-table queries instead of requiring an index per predicate.
N+1 queries are forbidden.
Limit query result scope; unbounded result sets are forbidden.
Bound batch read/write size rather than loading all data at once.
Do not rely on Open Session in View to hide JPA lazy loading; design aggregate fetch boundaries and read projections explicitly.
Explicitly configure the correct MyBatis-Plus database type; fail startup on unsupported types.
Keep custom interceptor order deterministic and verify it cannot bypass pagination or naming rules.

At the persistence-adapter boundary, translate a known business unique-constraint conflict into an explicit domain/application exception or, after verifying equivalent existing data, an idempotent success; do not leak the database exception.
A shared `DataIntegrityViolationException` catch may cover JPA and Spring-translated MyBatis `DuplicateKeyException`, which is a subclass of it.

After the shared catch, confirm the violation is the intended unique constraint by known constraint name, SQLState/vendor code, or a business-key reread; never classify not-null, foreign-key, or check-constraint violations as duplicate keys.
To catch a JPA unique-constraint failure inside an adapter, flush within that catch boundary; otherwise translate the deferred exception at a boundary that covers transaction commit.

After a unique-constraint failure, never reread and report idempotent success using a failed or rollback-only transaction or an unreliable persistence context. Especially after JPA/Hibernate persistence exceptions, end the failed transaction before verifying existing outcomes through a valid new transaction or independent query boundary. A nested call inside the failed transaction alone is not recovery; propagate verification failures.

Record known uniqueness-conflict outcomes once at the translation boundary with constraint/scene, sanitized business key, and outcome; severity, aggregation, and audit exceptions follow logging rules.
Propagate unknown or unclassified integrity failures rather than treating them as business uniqueness conflicts or idempotent success.
Name shared MyBatis/MyBatis-Plus SQL fragment files `<Aggregate>SqlFragments.xml` with namespace `<service-package>.persistence.sql.<Aggregate>SqlFragments`.
Name concrete mapper XML files `<Aggregate>Mapper.xml`.
Reference shared SQL fragments under the persistence reuse rules and always use a fully qualified `refid`.
Name persistence queries by conditions, range, and ordering rather than by a single caller or use case.

Generate globally unique aggregate, domain-event persistence-envelope, integration-event, and distributed-data identifiers through the injected `LongIdGenerator`; do not use database auto-increment, random values, timestamp concatenation, or a business-owned generator.
Pass a stable, configured, low-cardinality ID-space name to `nextId(name)`; do not derive generator names from user input, request IDs, or per-record business keys.
Register and validate generator names and corresponding CosId configuration before deployment.
A missing generator fails startup or its use case; never silently fall back to local algorithms or database auto-increment.

Generate aggregate and other business identifiers through framework ports in application/infrastructure and pass them into domain. Domain must not depend on `LongIdGenerator`, CosId, or starter types.
Domain-event persistence identifier generation follows the canonical EventStore and Envelope identity rule in service layering.
Treat generated IDs as unique and trend-increasing only; do not assume they are contiguous, gap-free, strictly chronological, or safe to decode into business meaning.

Non-Long string identifiers such as UUIDs or external identities are outside `LongIdGenerator`; never invent business-owned generation algorithms, and document their source in the project domain document.
Non-Long domain identifier types follow the layered-service project-level `EntityId` base constraints.
Manage node or machine identity and clock-rollback policy in shared infrastructure configuration; business modules must not override or hard-code node identity.

During the development phase, write and run only unit tests and module-contract tests; the code is not yet stable, so do not write or run integration tests during development and never substitute them for unit tests.
Keep unit and module contract tests in the tested module's `src/test`.
Verify observable behavior and public contracts rather than unnecessary implementation details.
In unit tests, mock only injected external collaborators; do not partially mock or spy on the subject under test.
Extract test support only for stable and meaningful reuse; do not create a common test base merely to remove small duplication.
Name unit and module contract tests `*Test`.
Run unit and module contract tests with Maven Surefire in the test phase.
Name test methods `should<ExpectedBehavior>` to state the observable behavior directly.
Every service declares a project documentation entry that routes each task to the required authoritative documents.
Every business service keeps `docs/DOMAIN.md` as the authoritative bounded-context document for domain language, rules, errors, events, and API business semantics.
Every project provides root `README.md` and `docs/RESPONSIBILITIES.md`.
An infrastructure project that owns a real domain should provide `docs/DOMAIN.md`; a pure library does not need one.

The documents required for the project type are a floor, not the full set; key infrastructure capabilities or external dependencies may have separate authoritative documents routed by the project documentation entry, with short names.

`README.md` is the project map answering what the project is, how to build, run, and verify it, where modules live, and where to read more; it must not carry responsibility philosophy or domain rules, and capability delivery status stays as a one-line overview linking to `docs/RESPONSIBILITIES.md`.
`docs/RESPONSIBILITIES.md` defines owned/unowned responsibilities, collaboration contracts, and delivery extent; it is the single home for cross-service collaboration contracts.
Each unowned responsibility listed in the responsibility document must identify its owner.

`docs/DOMAIN.md` is the domain design answering how the domain is modeled, carrying ubiquitous language, models, invariants, use cases, domain events and errors, and layering; it must not carry deployment or runtime configuration, delivery status, or other services' responsibilities.

Each side writes its half of a cross-service contract in its own `docs/RESPONSIBILITIES.md` and links to the other: the caller owns end-to-end flow and the callee owns endpoint contract and consumption semantics. Never duplicate the same contract table or flow.
When a cross-service contract changes, both sides update their owned content together.
Reference the other side's authoritative document by link instead of copying its content.

skills.name: develop-distributed
skills.when: Implementing or reviewing cross-instance locking, reliable event publication, message consumption, partitioning, dead letters, delayed messages, or related failure handling.

rules.text: A distributed lock is never the sole correctness guarantee; handle expiry, pauses, partitions, and duplicate execution and use the independent correctness protection defined by the persistence concurrency rule.
Use the injected `LockExecutor` and `LockContext(waitTime, lockNames)`; business code must not depend directly on Redisson, Spring Integration Redis Lock, or raw Redis lock commands.
Business lock key segments together identify the same contended resource stably; never use random keys or multiple formats for one resource.

`LockExecutor` internally normalizes business segments through `ResourceNameResolver`, including `String.join` and namespace injection; callers pass business segments and never resolve or pre-prefix keys.
Lock key segments contain no sensitive data under the logging definition.
Bound wait time by business SLA; never wait indefinitely or spin without backoff.
Prefer immediate lock acquisition by default.
On acquisition failure return an explicit retryable, conflict, or degradation outcome.
Cover the normal critical-section upper bound with a lease and safety margin; bound critical-section duration even with automatic renewal.
Restrict critical sections to necessary read/modify/write work, excluding avoidable remote calls, large batch processing, and long transactions.
Use `LockExecutor`-managed execution so only the owning flow unlocks in `finally`; do not transfer lock ownership across threads.

When a lock protects database work, acquire it before opening the protected transaction and release it only after commit or rollback completes. A method returning is not proof of transaction completion; verify actual boundaries with outer transactions and proxies.
Define one global acquisition order for multiple locks; when one aggregate or stable business key can represent the resource, use that single lock instead of expanding the lock set.
Application submits integration events only through `IntegrationEventOutbox`, without direct RabbitMQ templates or broker APIs.
Commit business state and outbox rows atomically in the same local transaction; direct publication must not replace reliable outbox semantics.
Trigger an outbox publication signal only after transaction commit.
A stable integration-event contract includes globally unique event ID, event type, aggregate type, aggregate ID, and occurrence time.
Never directly serialize domain entities as integration events; use the distinct domain/integration type boundary defined by service layering.
An outbox batch contains events from one aggregate and preserves batch sequence; split cross-aggregate events and never promise global ordering.
When aggregate ordering is required, use its stable ID as the partition key; do not use random or mutable keys and do not depend on global ordering.
Configure and validate destinations, partition counts, weights, and routing algorithms centrally at startup; business code must not create unmanaged destinations dynamically.
Before changing a partition count or routing algorithm, assess in-flight messages and ordering impact and define a migration plan.
Evolve event contracts backward-compatibly; new fields need compatible defaults, while deletion, rename, or semantic changes require a versioned migration.
Design consumers for at-least-once delivery and deduplicate by event ID or a stable business idempotency key; never assume a broker, outbox, or listener delivers once.
Commit completed-consumption deduplication and local business writes atomically in the same transaction; never mark consumed before separate fallible writes.
For nontransactional external effects, use a recoverable idempotency protocol preventing missed processing or duplicated side effects on retries.
Acknowledge only after business processing and local transaction success.
On consumer failure, use classified bounded retries and backoff.
Route unrecoverable messages or those exceeding retry thresholds to dead-letter or manual handling.
Listeners deserialize, validate, enter idempotency control, and must not swallow failures before acknowledgement; their layer responsibility follows the interfaces rules.
Use delayed messages only for error-tolerant retries, reminders, and auxiliary flows, never as precise timers or the sole guarantee of a core-business deadline.
On delayed-message arrival recheck state and idempotency; expired or completed work must not repeat side effects.
Use `DelayedOperations` with an explicit delay and keep RabbitMQ delayed-topology details out of business code.
When at-least-once delayed delivery is required, use a quorum configuration supporting that semantics.
Validate delay levels, tick, and maximum TTL against supported ranges at startup.
Monitor publication confirms/returns, outbox backlog, retries, consumer lag, and dead-letter counts.
Trace message processing with event ID, aggregate ID, and destination.

skills.name: develop-compensation
skills.when: Designing, implementing, or reviewing compensation, reconciliation, repair, cleanup, batch recovery, or fallback workflows

rules.text: Use compensation workflows only for fallback, compensation, reconciliation, repair, cleanup, and batch work; core real-time correctness must not depend on timely compensation execution.

Keep job, message, startup-recovery, and manual triggers as thin entry adapters that delegate to application use cases or shared infrastructure recovery services; trigger adapters contain no domain rules.
Jobs must be reentrant, retryable, and idempotent rather than assuming one trigger; data-writing effects follow the persistence concurrency rule.

When one resource needs a single processing flow, converge execution through stable mutually exclusive ownership; a shard key must map stably to the resource, use a distributed lock when sharding alone is not exclusive, and retain independent idempotency or concurrency protection for writes.
Use bounded pages or shards with stable sorted cursors, bounded batch size, and bounded runtime; never load all data at once.
Never hold a transaction across multiple batches.

Persist a recoverable checkpoint after each committed batch and resume from a recorded committed boundary. If a batch commits before its checkpoint is saved, replay must remain safe without amplifying side effects.
Parameters carry only validated business scope, cursors, or switches and fail fast when missing or invalid.
Job parameters must not contain secrets.
Configure execution timeouts, alerts, log retention, and failure handling.
Log job name, executor, shard, batch, processed count, and outcome; follow logging rules for sensitive data.
An XXL-JOB scheduler implementation module provides only the trigger entry and framework adaptation and contains no compensation rule or use-case orchestration.
Supply XXL-JOB admin address, namespace, port, access token, and enablement through environment configuration; production must not depend on starter defaults for critical connectivity.

skills.name: test-integration
skills.when: Writing, running, or reviewing integration tests in the smoke-test phase

rules.text: Write and execute integration tests only in the smoke-test phase to verify cross-module collaboration and real infrastructure behavior after code stabilization; development-phase testing follows the unit-test rules.

Tests of real implementation collaboration across modules, full auto-configuration, real databases, or real middleware are integration tests; merely referencing another module's interface or DTO is insufficient.
Put service integration tests in the architecture-defined standalone test module, never in a production module.
Prefer Testcontainers for isolated and repeatable real-infrastructure scenarios.

When integration tests use containers, prefer an officially maintained lightweight image variant when its functionality, version, and target architecture satisfy the test; use the standard image only when the lightweight variant lacks required tools or capabilities.
Confirm that each image manifest supports the target architectures of local development and CI runners.
Prefer one multi-architecture image that supports both local development and CI runners.
Prefer self-contained integration scenarios, with containers, test application, configuration, probes, and lifecycle management in the corresponding `*IT`.
Name integration tests `*IT`; method naming follows unit-test naming rules.
Run integration tests with Maven Failsafe in integration-test and verify phases.
Prefer `@Testcontainers` and `@Container` to manage external infrastructure.
Release application contexts, executors, containers, and other created resources in `@AfterEach` or an equivalent lifecycle boundary.
Every integration test has same-named documentation covering its purpose, conditions, execution, manual observation steps, observation entry points, and expected result.
A standalone test module README contains only coverage, environment requirements, unified execution, report location, and documentation index.
Put detailed integration scenarios in the standalone test module's `docs/<TestClass>.md`.
Integration tests must allow manual observation of the key process and final result; automatic assertions or source reading alone are insufficient.
In the smoke-test phase, exercise the centralized masking implementation for every supported sensitive-data type and verify its output format.
In the smoke-test phase, prove that production logging emits no DEBUG records and exposes no plain-text sensitive data at any level.
Use a real database or Testcontainers in the smoke-test phase to cover schema constraints, naming strategy, transaction rollback, concurrency conflicts, stable pagination, and critical query plans.
When one repository contract has alternative implementations, run the same contract tests against each implementation in the smoke-test phase and verify equivalent observable behavior.
In the smoke-test phase, verify consecutive generation, isolation between generator names, and fast failure for a missing name.
For multi-instance deployment, verify that node identities do not conflict and clock rollback follows configured policy.
Use real Redis in the smoke-test phase to verify exclusion, acquisition failure, exceptional release, lease or renewal, and namespace isolation.
In a concurrent-write smoke test, prove both that one business result takes effect and that a database uniqueness constraint blocks a duplicate that bypasses the lock.
Use a real broker in the smoke-test phase to cover post-commit publication, publication retry, duplicate delivery, aggregate ordering, dead letters, and delayed-delivery tolerance.
Exercise database-commit/broker-unavailable, interrupted-consumer, and backlog-recovery failures in the smoke-test phase.
In the smoke-test phase, cover duplicate triggers, recovery after a partial-batch failure, concurrent instances, empty data, and invalid parameters.
When an actual trigger technology such as XXL-JOB is used, verify executor registration, namespace isolation, timeout, and failure alerts in the smoke-test phase.

skills.when: Planning or applying coordinated standards-driven layered service refactors

skills.name: update-standards
skills.when: Reconciling Markdown standards changes with catalog.json and preparing a standards release
